# Japan As Number One: Lessons for America

Image: Front CoverEzra F. VogeliUniverse, Jun 1, 1999 - Social Science - 272 pages Based on the most up-to-date sources, as well as extensive research and direct observation, Japan as Number One analyze the island nation's development into one of the world's most effective industrial powers, in terms of not only economic productivity but also its ability to govern efficiently, to educate its citizens, to control crime, to alleviate energy shortages, and to lessen pollution. Ezra Vogel employs criteria that America has traditionally used to measure success in his thoughtful semonstration of how and why Japanese institutions have coped far more effectively than their American counterparts.

POLITICS

Japan as Number 1  
LESSONS FOR AMERICA  
Ezra F. Vogel

At the same time it was developing into the world’s most competitive industrial power, Japan was solving the internal problems that the United States now faces. Isn’t it about time, Ezra Vogel asks in this wide-ranging work, that we learn something from the competitor overtaking us?

“Japan as Number One: Lessons for America. The very title will blow the minds of many Americans. But unquestionably Japan today has a more smoothly functioning society and an economy that is running rings around ours. Vogel’s fascinating book will help explain this best organized and most dynamic of all major modern nations. It also has some hints that might help us with our problems. If the Japanese could learn from us with such profit in the past, perhaps there is something that we now need to learn from them.”  
—Edwin O. Reischauer

“An important and challenging book.”

The government is run by a stable elite bureaucracy ""able to provide predictable leadership for the private sector"" without, like its French counterpart, alienating the public--a matter, basically, of ""root binding,"" of involving every interested party in a decision. (The Carter administration energy plan, Vogel notes, was ""brilliantly argued"" but unsupported; the Japanese consulted with everyone, moved slowly, and made progress.) Politics, based on the solidarity of multipurpose groups, operates so as to give everyone a fair share (whereas in the U.S. ""fair play"" results in the winner taking all). Large companies, funded chiefly by banks (and only incidentally by stock-holders), are not under pressure to seek short-term profits--and their lifetime employees have a long-term stake too. (Thus, costly worker-displacing technologies are readily introduced.) This litany of Japanese successes--which extends to education (demonstrably superior through grade nine), welfare (short on entitlement, long on self-reliance), and crime control (spectacular--thanks to a high degree of social control)--sometimes gets to sounding like the description of a machine whose every part functions perfectly. In his wrap-up, Vogel does note Japan's glaring imperfections, like ""smothering individuality""; but he fails to confront the extent to which Japanese success depends on the very traits most inimical to the West. A stimulating work nonetheless--and an eye-opener for anyone who still thinks the Japanese succeed through double-dealing and low wages.
